title: Hugging Face Examples
description: Small Hugging Face examples from the lessons. Each example links back to its explanation and practice task.

examples.title: Find the different Hugging Face tools
examples.description: Hugging Face includes a Hub for shared resources and libraries used in local programs. These are related tools with different jobs.
examples.code:
Hub: pages for models, datasets and other resources
Datasets library: load and transform data tables
Tokenizers library: turn text into token IDs
Transformers library: work with many model architectures

examples.title: Read a model card before use
examples.description: A model card explains a shared model's intended use, training information, checks and limits. Also read its licence and files before deciding to use it.
examples.code:
Check the model page for:
Task and supported languages
Licence and use conditions
Training and evaluation notes
Known limits
Files and code required to load it

examples.title: Make a dataset from a dictionary
examples.description: A Dataset holds rows with named columns. from_dict creates a dataset from equally sized lists, one list per column.
examples.code:
from datasets import Dataset
data = Dataset.from_dict({"text": ["moon glows", "sun shines", "stars twinkle"], "length": [2, 2, 2]})
print(data.num_rows, data.column_names)

examples.title: Select rows by position
examples.description: select makes a dataset containing chosen row positions. Positions begin at zero, and the requested order is preserved.
examples.code:
from datasets import Dataset
data = Dataset.from_dict({"text": ["moon", "sun", "stars"]})
small = data.select([2, 0])
print(list(small["text"]))

examples.title: Filter using a condition
examples.description: filter keeps rows for which a function returns True. The function receives a row and checks the condition you chose.
examples.code:
from datasets import Dataset
data = Dataset.from_dict({"text": ["moon", "sun", "stars"]})
long_words = data.filter(lambda row: len(row["text"]) > 3)
print(list(long_words["text"]))

examples.title: Add a calculated column
examples.description: map applies a function to rows and returns an updated dataset. Returning a dictionary can add named fields.
examples.code:
from datasets import Dataset
data = Dataset.from_dict({"text": ["moon", "sun"]})
with_lengths = data.map(lambda row: {"characters": len(row["text"])})
print(list(with_lengths["characters"]))

examples.title: Split data for later checks
examples.description: train_test_split divides a dataset into training and test parts. A seed makes this split repeatable for the same data and tool behaviour.
examples.code:
from datasets import Dataset
data = Dataset.from_dict({"text": ["a", "b", "c", "d", "e", "f"]})
parts = data.train_test_split(test_size=2, seed=7)
print(parts["train"].num_rows, parts["test"].num_rows)

examples.title: Build a tiny word tokenizer
examples.description: A tokenizer turns text into pieces and IDs. WordLevel uses whole pieces from a supplied vocabulary. Whitespace splits this simple sentence into words.
examples.code:
from tokenizers import Tokenizer
from tokenizers.models import WordLevel
from tokenizers.pre_tokenizers import Whitespace

tokenizer = Tokenizer(WordLevel({"[PAD]": 0, "[UNK]": 1, "moon": 2, "glows": 3}, unk_token="[UNK]"))
tokenizer.pre_tokenizer = Whitespace()
encoded = tokenizer.encode("moon glows")
print(encoded.tokens, encoded.ids)

examples.title: Recognise an unknown token
examples.description: When a piece is missing from this WordLevel vocabulary, the tokenizer uses its unknown marker. It does not invent a new learned word entry.
examples.code:
from tokenizers import Tokenizer
from tokenizers.models import WordLevel
from tokenizers.pre_tokenizers import Whitespace

tokenizer = Tokenizer(WordLevel({"[PAD]": 0, "[UNK]": 1, "moon": 2, "glows": 3}, unk_token="[UNK]"))
tokenizer.pre_tokenizer = Whitespace()
encoded = tokenizer.encode("boat glows")
print(encoded.tokens, encoded.ids)

examples.title: Decode IDs into text
examples.description: Decoding maps known token IDs back to text. Tokenization may not preserve every detail of original spacing, so test exact-text needs carefully.
examples.code:
from tokenizers import Tokenizer
from tokenizers.models import WordLevel
from tokenizers.pre_tokenizers import Whitespace

tokenizer = Tokenizer(WordLevel({"[PAD]": 0, "[UNK]": 1, "moon": 2, "glows": 3}, unk_token="[UNK]"))
tokenizer.pre_tokenizer = Whitespace()
print(tokenizer.decode([2, 3]))

examples.title: Pad a sequence and inspect its mask
examples.description: Padding adds filler tokens to reach a chosen length. An attention mask marks real tokens with 1 and padding with 0 in this encoding.
examples.code:
from tokenizers import Tokenizer
from tokenizers.models import WordLevel
from tokenizers.pre_tokenizers import Whitespace

tokenizer = Tokenizer(WordLevel({"[PAD]": 0, "[UNK]": 1, "moon": 2, "glows": 3}, unk_token="[UNK]"))
tokenizer.pre_tokenizer = Whitespace()
tokenizer.enable_padding(length=4, pad_id=0, pad_token="[PAD]")
encoded = tokenizer.encode("moon glows")
print(encoded.ids, encoded.attention_mask)

examples.title: Save and reload a local tokenizer
examples.description: A tokenizer can save its settings as a JSON file. Reloading that file restores the local vocabulary and processing rules.
examples.code:
from tokenizers import Tokenizer
from tokenizers.models import WordLevel
from tokenizers.pre_tokenizers import Whitespace

tokenizer = Tokenizer(WordLevel({"[PAD]": 0, "[UNK]": 1, "moon": 2, "glows": 3}, unk_token="[UNK]"))
tokenizer.pre_tokenizer = Whitespace()
tokenizer.save("practice-tokenizer.json")
restored = Tokenizer.from_file("practice-tokenizer.json")
print(restored.encode("moon glows").ids)
